source_title: Live: ASX set to edge up despite $US500b Alphabet share slump overnight
source_excerpt:
Cryptocurrency assets have lost value on Friday after a major attack on the Binance crypto exchange.
Tech giant Google and its owner, Alphabet, lost more than half a trillion US dollars on Thursday night amid worries that AI would subsume its advertising business, the largest one-day fall in the company's history.
But the ASX200 still gained ground on Friday, and it finished the week 1.78 per cent higher.
See how the day unfolded on the ABC's markets and business blog.
Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.
Australian dollar: +0.1% at 70.34 US cents

All four major banks now expect the RBA to lift the cash rate from 4.6% to 4.85% next week.
We'll be back on Monday, and hopefully see you then.

As technology changes, criminals' methods change with them.
It's not as though your meagre bank savings as a child weren't still under threat. Australia had its fair share of bank robbers in days gone past who specialised in knocking down walls, cutting through floors, and picking their way into bank vaults to steal cash. Some of them dressed pretty well when they did it too.
The Australian movie Two Hands (with the late Heath Ledger) had a famous scene of a bank robbery and a Holden used as a getaway car, in the days when cash was still widely used. But it's the type of movie scene that wouldn't make much sense these days, since we've shifted the bulk of our currency into digital 1s and 0s.

Lawyer for First Guardian director David Anderson responds
The lawyer acting for David Anderson, who corporate watchdog ASIC is taking to court over alleged failures in running the First Guardian investment fund, says that they will respond in due course.
"We have been served with ASIC's proceedings only earlier today," Dan Mackay of Mackay Chapman said.
"The statement of claim runs to over 150 pages in length. It contains at present unproven allegations of fact and law.
"Notwithstanding its contents or what might be included in ASIC's media release, the matters remain, as they have since ASIC commenced its investigation, to be proven by ASIC.
"We will review the statement of claim in the coming days, but as you would expect, we have no comment to provide at this time."

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has provided the ABC with an updated statement:
"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified.
"The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3 billion. We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.
"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company’s funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.
"As an immediate precaution, Binance has: - temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; - revoked the affected address authorisation; - engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
"Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Corporate watchdog sues Falcon Capital directors
ASIC is suing the directors of the First Guardian fund alleging hundreds of millions of dollars of Australians' superannuation were exposed to "high-risk, undocumented and conflicted investments".
ASIC said it had commenced civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against former managing director and CEO David Anderson and former executive chairman and chief investment officer Simon Selimaj, alleging "serious and widespread failures in the management and oversight of First Guardian".
"ASIC is also seeking leave of the court to commence civil penalty proceedings against Falcon Capital, the responsible entity for First Guardian," it said.
ASIC alleges that between August 2019 and April 2025, more than 6,000 Australians invested more than $600 million in First Guardian, largely from their superannuation.
ASIC alleges Falcon Capital invested around $270 million through unregistered underlying funds it controlled, with substantial amounts paid to a range of entities and ventures without appropriate safeguards.
ASIC alleges Falcon Capital made investments with "inadequate documentation, insufficient security, inadequate due diligence, and unmanaged conflicts of interest".
These included investments in hospitality businesses and technology ventures in which Mr Anderson had a personal interest, as well as payments of at least $57 million to entities controlled by Mr Anderson or Mr Selimaj.
"Hundreds of millions of dollars were allegedly channelled into high-risk and conflicted investments with inadequate scrutiny, oversight, or governance and without regard to members' best interests," ASIC chair Sarah Court said.
"These were Australians' retirement savings, yet ASIC alleges millions of dollars were handed over before contracts were even in place, including for investments linked to those running the fund."
In December, under a deal with the corporate regulator, Netwealth reimbursed about $100 million to about 1,000 First Guardian investors who invested through its platform.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it had frozen $3 billion in crypto assets as it investigated a potential security breach.
"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said.
The market impact of the possible hacking, which could be the largest-ever crypto heist according to analytics firm Chainalysis, was felt immediately in early Asian trading on Friday.
Bitcoin dropped about 2% to a six-week low of $77,646
Ether fell around 2% to a two-month low of $2,238.76
BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down more than 8% over the past 24 hours at $694, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.
Binance said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has more than 335 million registered users globally and had about $160 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2024 annual report.
"It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.
"My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges; [it is] becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size."
Binance said it was conducting security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It added user funds remained safe and that teams were reviewing the incident.
The exchange also temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said the incident began around 4:30pm EDT (2030 GMT) and appeared to be ongoing.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.

Japan's Nikkei 225 is trading sharply lower today, losing as much as 3% in value today.
The index is being weighed down by technology stocks (-4.58%), utilities (-2.72%), and basic materials (-2.3%).
Japan's Nikkei share average dropped as much as 3% on Friday, led by chip-related stocks, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of spending to fund the AI boom.
Tokyo tracked overnight losses on Wall Street , and were given additional impetus by late earnings from Amazon.com and Intel that showed massive cash burns , sending shares in those companies and their peers sharply lower in extended trading.
"This can be seen as a sign of growing concerns regarding the profitability of AI investments, which is weighing on share prices," said Maki Sawada, an equities strategist at Nomura Securities.
"The Japanese stock market is being affected by this fall in US technology shares."
The Nikkei was down 2.8% [after lunch] after earlier slumping 3%, led lower by chip equipment heavyweights Advantest and Tokyo Electron, which plunged 9.1% and 5.6%, respectively.
Trading has been volatile this week as earnings reports from Japan, the US and South Korea triggered sharp swings in technology stocks.
For the week, the Nikkei remains up 0.2%.
Interest rates, exchange rates and economic pressures
The Fed holds, the European Central Bank held, Bank of New Zealand same story and now — the Bank of Japan set to follow suit.
Analysts are forecasting the BOJ will keep interest rates at 1.25% despite elevated inflation pressures, with an 80% chance of a December hike.
Of course, this happens as the war in the Middle East rumbles on, pushing up fuel prices and shipping costs.
"I think this is just a temporary pause. The global tightening cycle is still going to continue and that will continue to be a driver for FX markets. The big question is as we enter 2027, whether or not we might end up with potentially even more hikes if the inflation stays elevated," said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ.
US Treasury bond yields hit their lowest in a month, with the greenback up 0.3% this month against a basket of peers.
Elsewhere, oil prices remained elevated, with Brent crude futures on track for an 11.5% gain in their fourth straight month of gains, the longest streak in over two years.
As for interest rate decisions, it's the Brits and us who will find out next week.

A few months ago, the CommBank Household Spending Insights index , which tracks real-time spending across the economy, noted a clear divergence in consumption patterns by age in Australia this year.
It said Australians aged 65 and over had recorded the strongest annual spending growth of any age group, up 10.1% in the year to June 2026.
It found spending growth among 18- to 24-year-olds nearly halved over the year, easing from 9.9% in June 2025 to 5.4% in June 2026 — the biggest slowdown of any age group .
Growth for 25- to 34-year-olds was the weakest of all at just 4.2%, with 35 to 44 and 45- to 54-year-olds close behind at 4.5% each.
"These groups are more likely to have a mortgage, making them more sensitive to higher interest rates," Belinda Allen, CBA's Head of Australian Economics, said.
The 55 to 64 years age group bucked the trend, with growth actually picking up from 5.8% to 6.2% over the year.
Since that release, the Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates by another 25 basis points (in September), and markets expect another rate rise next week.
